cards.title: LangChain is a *function call*. LangGraph is a *while loop with a save button*.
cards.body: A LangChain chain runs top to bottom once: prompt → model → parser, done. A LangGraph graph keeps a State dict alive, lets nodes jump backwards, and can persist that dict between runs. If your pseudocode has `while` or `if ... goto`, it is a graph.
cards.why: Interview framing: 'LangChain for DAGs, LangGraph for cyclic, stateful, resumable workflows.'

cards.title: Same model, same tools — only the *control flow* changes on each rung.
cards.body: Rung 1: a chain calls the model once. Rung 2: an agent lets the model decide the next call in a loop. Rung 3: multi-agent gives several loops their own state and a router. Nothing new appears except who decides what happens next.
cards.why: This is the one mental model that connects chains, agents and multi-agent systems — the thing that felt disconnected before.

diagram.caption: Each rung hands more of the control flow to the model.

cards.title: Split on structure first, size second.
cards.body: `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` tries separators in order: paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, then characters. It only falls to the next separator when a piece is still too big. So chunks respect document structure wherever they can.
cards.why: Naive fixed-size splitting cuts sentences in half; the embedding of half a sentence is garbage.

code.src:
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],  # tried in order
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(doc_text)

cards.title: The model only sees what you *typed*, never what the function *does*.
cards.body: A tool's name, docstring and argument schema are serialized into the prompt. The body is invisible to the model. Pick the fix for the scenario below.

quiz.question: Your tool `lookup(id: str)` is correct but the agent keeps passing customer *names* instead of IDs. Cheapest fix?
options: Add a Field description: 'Numeric customer ID like "C-10422", not a name'
Catch the error inside lookup() and search by name
quiz.explain: The model never saw that `id` meant a specific format — it only saw `id: str`. Field descriptions are the cheapest lever because they change what the model reads before it decides. Fixing it inside the function hides the problem and still costs a wasted tool call.

cards.title: `create_agent` is ReAct with the loop already written.
cards.body: You give it a model and tools; it builds the model → tools → model cycle and the single exit. Everything you learned about ReAct is still there — you just don't hand-write the conditional edge.
cards.why: Know the hand-written version for interviews; use the prebuilt one in production.

code.src:
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
    tools=[search, calculator],
    system_prompt="Answer with numbers, cite the tool you used.",
)
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "GDP of Spain / population?")]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)

cards.title: A checkpoint is written after *every* node, not just at the end.
cards.body: Each super-step saves the full State under the thread_id. That is why you can resume mid-run after a crash, time-travel to a past step, or fork a thread from any checkpoint — the history is already there.
cards.why: Saves the 'I lost 40 tool calls when the pod restarted' incident.

cards.title: The supervisor's job is to *route*, not to *do*.
cards.body: A good supervisor node has one responsibility: decide which worker runs next, or finish. Workers own the real tools. Pick the design smell below.

quiz.question: Your supervisor has 14 tools bound to it and the workers have 2 each. Latency doubled. What went wrong?
options: The supervisor is doing the work itself instead of delegating, so every step pays for a 14-tool prompt
quiz.explain: Every tool schema is prompt tokens on every call. A supervisor carrying 14 tools is a fat agent with a routing side-hustle. Give the supervisor zero tools (or just a `handoff` schema) and push the tools down to the specialists.

cards.title: Trace → dataset → eval is one pipeline, not three products.
cards.body: Traces capture real inputs and outputs. You curate the interesting ones into a dataset. Evals replay that dataset against new versions. LangSmith owns the first two lanes; DeepEval or MLflow can own the third.
cards.why: The best eval datasets come from production traces, not from someone inventing test cases.

cards.title: Autolog LangChain once; every chain and agent call becomes a trace.
cards.body: `mlflow.langchain.autolog()` patches the LangChain callbacks so you get spans for prompts, models, tools and retrievers without decorating anything. Combine with `@mlflow.trace` for your own glue code.
cards.why: One line in your entrypoint beats remembering to decorate 30 functions.

cards.title: Send() fans out. A reducer fans back in.
cards.body: The planner emits one `Send` per item, each worker runs with its own private input, and their outputs are appended to a shared list by a reducer. Without the reducer the parallel writes would overwrite each other.
cards.why: Map-reduce is the shape behind batch summarisation, multi-query RAG, and this very feed.

diagram.caption: Send() = one arrow per item; the reducer merges the returns.

cards.title: interrupt() raises — the code after it does *not* run on the first pass.
cards.body: When a node calls `interrupt(payload)`, execution stops and the graph returns. On resume, the node re-runs from the top and `interrupt()` returns the resume value. Any side effect *before* the interrupt happens twice.

quiz.question: A node sends an email, then calls interrupt() for approval, then saves to DB. The human approves. What happens?
options: Email twice, save once — the node re-executes from the top on resume
quiz.explain: Resume replays the node; interrupt() now returns the approval instead of pausing. Put side effects *after* the interrupt, or move them to a separate node so the replay is cheap and idempotent.

cards.title: Build the eval before you tune the retriever.
cards.body: Changing chunk size, top-k or the embedding model without a scored dataset is guessing. Twenty question/ground-truth pairs plus faithfulness, answer relevancy and context recall turn every change into a number you can compare.
cards.why: The single habit that separates a RAG demo from a RAG system.

cards.title: Pull prompts by *tag*, not by *latest*.
cards.body: LangSmith prompt hub lets you push a prompt, then reference it as `name:production`. Code deploys and prompt deploys are decoupled: promote a prompt by moving the tag, roll back the same way.
cards.why: `latest` in production means someone editing a prompt in the UI at 5pm changes your app's behaviour at 5:01.

code.src:
from langsmith import Client

client = Client()
prompt = client.pull_prompt("support-triage:production")  # pinned by tag
chain = prompt | model
# promote: push a new commit, then move the tag in the UI or via client

cards.title: A deployed graph is an *assistant*; a run lives on a *thread*.
cards.body: LangGraph Server exposes your graph as an assistant (graph + config). Clients create a thread, then start runs on it. The server handles the checkpointer, queues and streaming, so your graph code stays identical to local.
cards.why: Thread = conversation ID. Same thread_id you used with the checkpointer locally.

cards.title: Sub-agents get a *fresh* context window — that is the whole point.
cards.body: A deep agent delegates a research task to a sub-agent that starts with an empty history and returns only a summary. The parent's context stays small no matter how many tool calls the child burned.
cards.why: Context bloat, not model IQ, is what kills long agent runs.

code.src:
from deepagents import create_deep_agent

researcher = {
    "name": "researcher",
    "description": "Deep-dive one question; return a 5-line summary.",
    "system_prompt": "Search widely, then summarise. Return only the summary.",
    "tools": [web_search],
}
agent = create_deep_agent(tools=[web_search], subagents=[researcher])

cards.title: Fail the build on a *score threshold*, not on exact strings.
cards.body: LLM outputs vary; your assertion should not. Run the dataset through an LLM judge, average the score, and assert it stays above a bar. Store the bar in one place so a regression is a red test, not a vibe.
cards.why: Exact-match asserts on LLM text flake every run and get deleted within a week.

code.src:
from deepeval import evaluate
from deepeval.metrics import FaithfulnessMetric
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase

def test_rag_faithfulness(golden_set):
    cases = [LLMTestCase(input=g.q, actual_output=rag(g.q),
                         retrieval_context=retrieve(g.q)) for g in golden_set]
    res = evaluate(cases, [FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.8)])
    assert res.pass_rate >= 0.9

cards.title: A router is a tiny classifier in front of two models.
cards.body: A cheap model (or even a regex) labels the request easy/hard. Easy goes to the small model, hard goes to the big one. Log the label so you can audit misroutes with evals later.
cards.why: Typical result: 60–80% of traffic on the cheap model with no measurable quality drop on the hard cases.

diagram.caption: Route by predicted difficulty; log the route for eval.

cards.title: Guardrails are nodes, not prompts.
cards.body: Put input checks (PII, injection, off-topic) in a node *before* the model and output checks (schema, policy) in a node *after*. Each check is deterministic code or a small classifier — never 'please don't' in the system prompt.
cards.why: A prompt instruction is a suggestion. A node that routes to END is a wall.

cards.title: Where does an output guardrail route when it fails?
cards.body: A failed check has three sane destinations: regenerate, hand to a human, or return a safe refusal. Pick the one that matches the scenario.

quiz.question: Your output checker finds the agent's reply leaks an internal URL. The user is waiting. Best route?
options: END with the reply anyway, log a warning
Loop back to the model with the violation in a system message, max 2 retries, then refuse
interrupt() and wait for a human on every leak
Delete the URL with regex and send
quiz.explain: A bounded retry with the violation explained usually fixes it in one pass and keeps latency sane. Unbounded human interrupts don't scale; regex scrubbing hides the real cause from your traces. Option 0 is the thing the guardrail exists to prevent.

cards.title: Attach a *price table* once; let a callback do the arithmetic.
cards.body: `usage_metadata` gives tokens, not money. A callback handler that multiplies by per-model rates turns every run into a dollar figure you can log, tag with thread_id, and alert on.
cards.why: Finance asks 'what does one conversation cost?' — this answers it per thread.

code.src:
from langchain_core.callbacks import BaseCallbackHandler

RATES = {"claude-sonnet-4-5": (3e-6, 15e-6)}  # $/input, $/output token

class Cost(BaseCallbackHandler):
    total = 0.0
    def on_llm_end(self, response, **kw):
        u = response.generations[0][0].message.usage_metadata
        i, o = RATES[kw["tags"][0]] if kw.get("tags") else (3e-6, 15e-6)
        self.total += u["input_tokens"] * i + u["output_tokens"] * o

cards.title: Treat a refusal as a *typed exception*, not as text to parse.
cards.body: Older code grepped the reply for 'I can't help'. With `ModelRefusalError` you catch one exception class, log it as a refusal in traces, and route the graph to a fallback — the same way you'd handle a rate limit.
cards.why: Refusals that look like normal answers silently poison your eval scores and your downstream parsers.

cards.title: Pin a baseline, then every eval run is a *diff*.
cards.body: Comparing two evaluation runs side by side answers the real question: did this change help? MLflow lines up per-example scores, latency and cost against the pinned baseline so regressions on a few rows don't hide behind a flat average.
cards.why: Averages lie; per-row diffs show the three questions your new prompt broke.

cards.title: A compiled graph is just a node.
cards.body: Compile a graph, then `add_node` it into a parent. If both share State keys, data flows automatically; if not, wrap it in a function that translates. This is how you package a RAG pipeline or a specialist agent as a reusable unit.
cards.why: Subgraphs are how multi-agent systems stay testable: each agent is a graph you can run alone.

code.src:
rag = rag_builder.compile()               # has keys: question, answer

parent = StateGraph(ParentState)          # also has question, answer
parent.add_node("rag", rag)               # shared keys flow through
parent.add_node("critic", critic_node)
parent.add_edge(START, "rag")
parent.add_edge("rag", "critic")
app = parent.compile()

cards.title: `updates`, `values`, `messages` — three answers to 'stream what?'
cards.body: `stream_mode="values"` emits the full State after each step; `"updates"` emits only the node's returned delta; `"messages"` emits LLM tokens as they arrive. Pick the one for the scenario.

quiz.question: You want a chat UI that shows tokens appearing live, plus a progress bar that ticks once per node. Which combination?
quiz.explain: stream_mode accepts a list. `messages` gives token-level chunks for the typing effect; `updates` fires once per node for the progress bar. `values` would resend the whole state each step — wasteful for a UI.

cards.title: langgraph 1.2.24 fixes `REMOVE_ALL_MESSAGES` in the messages reducer.
cards.body: Returning `RemoveMessage(id=REMOVE_ALL_MESSAGES)` tells `add_messages` to wipe history before appending what follows — the idiom for summarise-and-compact. 1.2.24 (Nov 20) fixes edge cases in that delta path and tolerates `None` checkpoints in `DeltaChannel`.
cards.why: This is the clean way to cap context: replace 40 messages with one summary message in a single node return.

cards.title: langchain-core 1.8.4: one `finish_reason` across providers.
cards.body: OpenAI says `stop`/`length`/`tool_calls`; Anthropic says `end_turn`/`max_tokens`/`tool_use`. 1.8.4 (Nov 19) standardises the finish reason on message-finish events, with langchain-openai 1.8.5 and langchain-anthropic 1.7.12 adopting it.
cards.why: A truncated answer (`length`) should trigger a retry with more budget — now you can detect it with one check regardless of model.

cards.title: Rejected tool calls now leave a *tagged* ToolMessage in the trace.
cards.body: When a human rejects a tool call in a HITL flow, LangChain fabricates a ToolMessage so the transcript stays valid. langchain-core 1.8.4 tags those synthetic messages with source metadata, so evals and traces can tell 'tool ran' from 'human said no'.
cards.why: Without the tag your tool-success metrics count human rejections as tool outputs.

cards.title: langchain-openai 1.8.4: a server error *mid-stream* is now retryable.
cards.body: Before, an error after the first token was terminal. 1.8.4 (Nov 19) classifies in-stream server errors as retryable, so `.with_retry()` and `max_retries` apply to streaming too.

quiz.question: Your streaming agent dies 200 tokens in with a 5xx. With 1.8.4 and max_retries=2, what does the user see?
options: The partial 200 tokens, then an error
A retried request; the stream restarts from the beginning
quiz.explain: Retry re-issues the request; there is no server-side cursor to resume from. Your UI should buffer or clear the partial output on retry. Token 201 resumption would need provider support that doesn't exist.

cards.title: LangSmith CLI: `langsmith feedback create` scores a run from the shell.
cards.body: The Nov 9–16 changelog adds `feedback create` and `feedback list`. Pair it with a script that reads your nightly eval results and you have feedback on production runs without touching the SDK.
cards.why: Lets a bash step in CI attach a score to the exact trace it tested.

code.src:
# shell, not Python — attach a score to a run after an offline check
langsmith feedback create --run-id "$RUN_ID" \
  --key faithfulness --score 0.92 \
  --comment "nightly deepeval judge"
langsmith feedback list --run-id "$RUN_ID"

cards.title: MLflow 3.18 runs *your* Python scorers on every new trace, automatically.
cards.body: Code-based online scorers (experimental) let you register a custom scorer and call `.start()`; the server then evaluates incoming traces in isolated job containers with networking disabled. Needs a SQL backend and `MLFLOW_SERVER_ENABLE_CUSTOM_SCORERS=true`.
cards.why: Closes the loop: offline eval logic becomes live monitoring without a second codebase.
